kzz7yh-a80049-d1e103.summary: Announces four questions on the third principal topic, the motion of an angel from place to place.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e119.summary: First question (text corrupt): whether an angel can move itself from place to place without an assumed body.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e124.summary: Second question: whether an angel moving from place to place must traverse the intervening medium.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e131.summary: Third question: whether it can traverse the medium in an instant.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e137.summary: Fourth question: whether there is a first change (mutatio prima) in its motion.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e146.summary: First objection: per Physics VI what is moved is partly in the starting term and partly in the end term, which cannot fit an indivisible angel; so it cannot move without an assumed body.
claims: Only divisible things can be moved (objection).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e166.summary: Second objection: per Physics VIII, every self-mover resolves into a per se mover and a per se moved part; an angel, though composed of actual and potential nature, has no per se mobile part.
claims: Self-movers must have a mover-part and a moved-part (objection).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e179.summary: Third objection: a local mover first traverses a space smaller than or equal to itself; nothing is smaller than an indivisible, and traversing equals would compose the continuum from indivisibles, which Physics VI disproves.
claims: Angelic motion would compose the continuum of indivisibles (objection).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e197.summary: Fourth objection: a divisible accident cannot be in an indivisible subject, and motion is a divisible accident.
claims: Motion cannot inhere in an indivisible subject (objection).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e205.summary: Fifth objection: motion is the act of the imperfect (Physics III); an angel is a perfect creature.
claims: Perfect creatures cannot be in motion (objection).
concepts: motion as act of the imperfect

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e212.summary: Sixth objection: Augustine (De Genesi ad litteram 8, cited by Lombard) says God moves spiritual creatures through time and corporeal ones through time and place, implying spirits do not move locally.
claims: Spiritual creatures move only through time (objection).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e228.summary: Sed contra: Damascene says angels, by the swiftness of their nature, quickly pass and operate in diverse places.
claims: Angels pass swiftly between places.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e237.summary: Second sed contra: motion is the act of a being in potency as such; an angel is in one determinate place and in potency to another.
claims: An angel in one place is in potency to another.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e246.summary: Third sed contra: at death the soul passes without a body to hell, purgatory or the empyrean, so likewise an angel can pass from place to place without a body.
claims: Separated souls move between places.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e255.summary: Richard's solution: taking 'motion' broadly as any change of place, successive or not (it will be shown to be successive), an angel can move. It is definitively in one determinate place, not everywhere, and not necessarily bound to any place since its conservation does not depend on place, so it can be in another. It can move itself because it is composed of actual and potential nature: mutable as a whole by reason of its potential element and moving as a whole by its actual element.
claims: An angel can change place since it is definitively located and not bound to any place.
An angel moves itself through its actual principle, while being movable through its potential principle.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e313.summary: Reply to the first objection: 'partly in each term' means having part of the starting term and part of the end term, a partibility relative to the terms, not in the mobile absolutely (as Avempace, reported by Averroes, held). An angel, though simple, is in a partible place and can so relate to both terms.
claims: The partibility required for motion can be relative to the terms of motion, not intrinsic to the mobile.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e344.summary: Reply to the second objection: the resolution of self-movers into mover and moved applies to corporeal things that determine themselves to motion, not to spirits, nor to heavy and light bodies, which are determined to motion by their generator.
claims: Aristotle's self-mover analysis applies only to corporeal self-movers.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e364.summary: Reply to the third objection: the principle of first traversing a smaller space refers not to the mobile's absolute quantity but to the place it can define; a moving angel first acquires a space smaller than its definable place.
claims: Angelic motion acquires spaces smaller than its definable place first.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e384.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: an accident whose parts do not coexist, like motion, can be in an indivisible subject by relation to something divisible, such as space.
claims: Successive accidents can inhere in indivisible subjects relative to divisible space.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e395.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: 'imperfect' there means a being in potency to something; an angel in one place is in potency to another.
claims: 'Imperfect' in the definition of motion means in potency.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e408.summary: Reply to the sixth objection: Augustine does not deny all local motion to spirits, only motion like that of bodies commensurated to space.
claims: Augustine denies only commensurate bodily motion to spirits.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e420.summary: First argument that an angel need not traverse the medium: Damascene says it is present where it operates, and it can refrain from operating in the medium.
claims: Angelic presence follows operation, so the medium can be skipped (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e440.summary: Second argument: between two places there are infinitely many parts, so traversing the medium would require traversing infinities.
claims: Traversal of a continuum requires traversing infinitely many parts (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e451.summary: Third argument: the soul's thought passes from Paris to Amiens without thinking of intermediate places; a fortiori an angel, being simpler, can skip the medium.
claims: Thought skips intermediate places (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e464.summary: Sed contra: per Physics V, the medium is what the changing thing reaches before the end term.
claims: Change passes through the medium before the end.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e478.summary: Second sed contra: per Physics VI, being moved precedes having been moved; having been moved is at the end term, so being moved occurs in the medium.
claims: Being moved occurs in the medium.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e489.summary: Reports two opinions: some hold that an angel may skip the medium at will because it is in place only by operation, a foundation already refuted; others hold that, since location is by simultas and applying itself to place is up to the angel's will, it may traverse or skip the medium as it pleases, which contradicts the common opinion of the doctors.
claims: The operation-based view of skipping the medium rests on a refuted premise.
The simultas-based voluntarist view contradicts the common opinion.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e531.summary: Richard's determination: a moving angel must pass through the medium, though not as bodies do, since it is not commensurated to the medium either actually or potentially.
claims: An angel must traverse the medium when moving.
An angel is not commensurated to the medium.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e540.summary: Reply to Damascene: he does not mean angels are in place only by operation, but that the angel makes itself present where it operates and could not operate immediately on a place unless present there.
claims: Immediate operation on a place requires presence.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e556.summary: Reply to the infinity argument: during motion the mobile occupies spaces equal to itself only potentially until the end; a moving angel defines no space actually; and traversing infinitely many potential parts is possible, unlike actual infinities.
claims: During motion, intermediate places are occupied only potentially.
Traversing a potential infinity is possible.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e569.summary: Reply to the thought analogy: the species of distant places in the soul are not distant from one another, though the places are, so thinking of one place and then another does not pass through distant species.
claims: Intelligible species of distant places are not themselves distant.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e587.summary: First argument for instantaneous traversal: changes of non-proportional movers are non-proportional; body and angel are non-proportional movers, and every time is proportional to every time, so the angel moves in no time.
claims: Non-proportional movers yield non-proportional motions (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e607.summary: Second argument: per Physics IV, motion through a void would not be successive; a plenum resists an angel no more than a void.
claims: Without resistance motion would be instantaneous (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e618.summary: Third argument: some changes from corporeal power are instantaneous through a medium, like illumination; a fortiori an angel's change from spiritual power.
claims: Illumination is instantaneous (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e629.summary: Fourth argument: Averroes reports Aristotle saying succession in local motion arises from resistance of medium to mobile or mobile to mover; neither applies to an angel.
claims: Succession arises only from resistance (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e646.summary: Fifth argument: Avicenna says the time of motion without impediment has no proportion to time with impediment, so such motion is in no time.
claims: Unimpeded motion is timeless (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e659.summary: Sixth argument: Damascene says angels are found 'confestim' wherever God commands; 'immediately' seems to mean instantly.
claims: Angels arrive immediately (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e668.summary: Sed contra: if an angel moved through the medium in an instant, the minimal measure, divine power could not move it faster, which is false since greater power moves the same mobile over the same space in less time.
claims: Instantaneous angelic motion would limit divine power.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e684.summary: Second sed contra: per Physics VI the divisibility of motion follows that of magnitude, and time divides as motion does; so motion through a divisible medium is in time.
claims: Motion through divisible magnitude takes divisible time.
concepts: isomorphism of magnitude, motion and time

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e704.summary: Third sed contra: Averroes says only a change that is the end of motion is indivisible; passage from rest to rest through a medium by finite power cannot be instantaneous.
claims: Finite power cannot effect instantaneous traversal.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e720.summary: Reports and rejects a view that an angel can traverse the medium instantly because its finite power infinitely exceeds an unresisting space, as a line exceeds a point. Richard replies that even without resistance from density, the divisibility of space as such prevents a limited power from transferring any mobile, corporeal or spiritual, instantaneously.
claims: Divisibility of space, not only resistance, prevents instantaneous motion by finite power.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e752.summary: Richard's determination: an angel cannot move through the medium instantaneously, for the reason just given and because every designated place in the medium is one where the angel could actually be definitively; passing through them only in potency mixed with act is successive transfer, which is not instantaneous.
claims: Angelic motion through the medium is successive, not instantaneous.
Passage through intermediate places in potency mixed with act is successive.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e778.summary: Reply to the first argument: though angelic and corporeal essences are non-proportional, their motive powers are proportional since both are finite.
claims: Finite motive powers are mutually proportional.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e794.summary: Reply to the second argument: Aristotle's claim concerns a void without any dimensions, corporeal or separate, where there would be no actual medium at all; he also holds that no body could be placed in a void of separate dimensions, so the authority is irrelevant.
claims: Aristotle's void argument concerns a dimensionless void with no medium.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e818.summary: Reply to the third argument: some deny that illumination is instantaneous, holding it occurs in imperceptible time (to be examined in Book II). Even granting it, illumination involves no single thing traversing the medium, since each part illumines the next, so it is not comparable to angelic motion.
claims: Illumination involves no single traversing mobile.
Whether illumination is instantaneous is disputed.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e847.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: succession is caused by resistance or by something that takes its place in causing succession, here the finitude of angelic power together with the divisibility of space.
claims: Finite power plus divisible space causes succession even without resistance.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e869.summary: Reply to Avicenna: the claim concerns time spent on motion due to resistance alone, not time due to dimension when resistance is removed; Aristotle's proportion of times to resistances is read likewise.
claims: Time of motion has components from resistance and from dimension.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e894.summary: Reply to Damascene: 'confestim' signifies a brief time, like 'statim', while an instant is no part of time; the sed contra arguments are conceded for their conclusion.
claims: 'Confestim' denotes brief time, not an instant.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e910.summary: First argument against a first change: per Physics VI, at the start of motion there is no first point at which it has changed; a first change would supply one.
claims: There is no first 'having changed' at the start of motion (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e928.summary: Second argument: Averroes says change has no beginning unless change and time were composed of indivisibles, which they are not.
claims: Change has no first part since time is not composed of indivisibles (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e944.summary: Third argument: Aristotle proves that before changing there is having-changed and before that changing, so there is no first change.
claims: Every change is preceded by change (argument).

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e951.summary: Sed contra: as time to instant and line to point, so motion to change; line begins with a point and time with an instant, so angelic motion begins with a change.
claims: Motion begins with an indivisible change.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e963.summary: Second sed contra: whatever has being after non-being begins; the beginning of motion cannot be motion since motion is endlessly divisible, so it is a change.
claims: The beginning of motion is a mutatio.

kzz7yh-a80049-d1e970.summary: Richard's solution: change, as 'going from one thing to another' (Gregory), can be considered as from something or as to something. As from something, there is a first change, since there is an indivisible from which the angel first departs. As to something, there is no first 'having changed' at the beginning: neither a divisible part (a part is acquired before the whole) nor an indivisible (indivisibles are not continuous or contiguous). At the end there is an indivisible terminus. Even moving into a contiguous space, nothing is acquired actually at the start without rest; Averroes says the beginning of change is potential and its end actual. The sed contra hold for change considered as 'from'; the point-line analogy fails since motion cannot actually have an initiating change 'into' something.
claims: As departure from a term, angelic motion has a first change.
As acquisition of a term, angelic motion has no first moment of having changed.
The beginning of transmutation is potential, its end actual.
concepts: terminus a quo and ad quem

kzz7yh-a80049-Dd1e142.summary: Question 1 holds that an angel can move itself from place to place without an assumed body. It is definitively in one place, not bound to any place by nature, and composed of actual and potential principles, so it is movable as potential and self-moving as actual. The replies reinterpret Aristotle's divisibility requirement as relative to the terms (with Avempace), restrict the self-mover analysis to bodies, and relate the 'smaller space first' principle to the angel's definable place. Motion, a successive accident, can be in an indivisible subject relative to space, 'imperfect' means in potency, and Augustine denies spirits only bodily, commensurate motion.
claims: Angels can move themselves locally without bodies.
Angelic self-motion rests on composition of act and potency.

kzz7yh-a80049-Dd1e416.summary: Question 2 holds that an angel moving between places must traverse the medium, though not as bodies do, since it is not commensurated to it. Richard rejects the view that angels can skip the medium because they are located only by operation, and also the voluntarist variant based on simultas. Damascene means only that immediate operation requires presence. The infinity of intermediate parts is traversable because they are occupied only potentially. The mind's leap from Paris to Amiens shows nothing, since species of distant places are not distant.
claims: Angelic motion passes through the medium.
Intermediate places are traversed only potentially.

kzz7yh-a80049-Dd1e583.summary: Question 3 denies that an angel traverses the medium instantaneously. Even with no resistance, the divisibility of space combined with the finitude of angelic power makes the motion successive. The angel also passes through intermediate places in potency mixed with act, each a place it could actually occupy definitively. Richard rejects the argument that finite power infinitely exceeds unresisting space. He replies that finite powers are proportional, that Aristotle's void lacks any medium, that illumination involves no single traversing mobile, and that time of motion stems from dimension as well as resistance. Damascene's 'confestim' means a brief time, not an instant.
claims: Angelic local motion is successive, in time.
Finite power and divisible space cause succession without resistance.

kzz7yh-a80049-Dd1e906.summary: Question 4 resolves whether angelic motion has a first change by distinguishing change as departure from a term and as acquisition of a term. There is a first change in departure, since the angel leaves an indivisible starting position. There is no first 'having changed' in acquisition, since neither a divisible nor an indivisible first acquisition is possible in a continuum. At the end there is an indivisible terminus. This reconciles Aristotle's denial of a first moment of change with the analogy of line and point, following Averroes's dictum that the beginning of change is potential and its end actual.
claims: Angelic motion has a first change as departure but not as acquisition.
The start of change is potential, its end actual.

kzz7yh-a80049.summary: Article 3 of I d.37 treats the local motion of angels in four questions, applying Aristotelian physics of the continuum to spiritual substances. An angel can move itself without a body, being definitively located, unbound to any place, and composed of act and potency. It must traverse the medium, though not commensurately, against the views that let it skip intervening space. Its motion is successive, not instantaneous, because finite power combined with the divisibility of space produces succession even without resistance. That motion has a first change considered as departure from the starting point, but no first moment considered as acquisition of the end term.
claims: Angels move themselves locally without bodies.
Angelic motion traverses the medium and is successive.
Finite power and divisible space suffice for succession without resistance.
Angelic motion has a first change as departure, not as acquisition.
